title: Moonlight, Skyglow and the Ageing Eye in a Visual Dawn Criterion: When Does a White Thread Become Distinct from a Black One?
content: For more than a billion people the daily fast of Ramadan begins at a moment that scripture defines by vision: when a white thread can be told apart from a black one at dawn. We compute this moment from the twilight illuminance and the Adrian visibility model, with its dependence on observer age, and then ask how the sky changes it. Under a clear, moonless, unpolluted sky, threads of 0.3 mm and 1 mm held at 40 cm become distinct at solar depressions of 8° and 12° for a 20-year-old observer and 1–2° later for a 70-year-old. In İstanbul this is 40–60 min before sunrise, against 91 min for the 18° of prayer calendars. A doubling of the twilight brightness moves the threshold by 0.7°–1.5°. Skyglow above about 0.01 lx, or the full and waning gibbous moon, keeps a 1 mm thread distinguishable to a young observer through the hours before dawn; in Ramadan 1448 AH (February–March 2027) this happens on eight of thirty mornings. Thin threads and older eyes are much less sensitive to the night sky. The literal test is therefore a measure of the sky and the observer as much as of the sun.
